consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same primary identification: Egypt symbolizes bondage to sin and the world-system opposed to God—the unredeemed condition out of which God delivers his people, grounded in the Exodus typology (Exodus 1–14; Deut 5:6; 1 Cor 10; Heb 11; Rev 11:8). Secondary alternatives include Egypt as false object of trust, place of refuge, proud imperial power, and eschatological recipient of grace. One response (A) lists as a minority alternative the reading of Revelation 11:8's 'Egypt' as a cipher for apostate Jerusalem.
book_summary: The book identifies Egypt as 'a covenant city in bondage under worldly rule'—specifically Jerusalem in covenant corruption—reading Revelation 11:8's spiritual name 'Egypt' as designating the great city where the Lord was crucified, i.e., apostate Jerusalem, supported by Matt 23:37 (Jerusalem kills the prophets), Gal 4:25 (Jerusalem 'is in bondage'), and Isa 1:10 (Sodom-language applied to Israel's rulers). The book explicitly flags the common teaching (bondage to sin / the world-system) as the view it departs from.
consensus_core_identification: Egypt = the world of sin and slavery external to God's people; the pagan world-system and unredeemed condition from which God redeems his own in an exodus pattern.
book_core_identification: Egypt = the covenant city itself (apostate Jerusalem) in bondage and covenant corruption under worldly rule—the symbol points inward at God's own covenant people gone corrupt, not outward at the pagan world.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus applies the Egypt symbol to the pagan world and the sinful condition outside the covenant; the book reclassifies the symbol's referent as the covenant community itself (Jerusalem) in a state of bondage and corruption. The shared element of 'bondage' is retained, but who is 'Egypt' is inverted: the consensus makes Egypt the oppressor-realm from which the covenant people exit; the book makes Egypt the covenant city that has become enslaved and prophet-killing.
material_contradiction: The consensus identification ('the world-system out of which God redeems his people') and the book's identification ('the covenant city in bondage') cannot both be the central sense of the symbol in the same context: one places Egypt outside the covenant as the domain of the unredeemed, the other places it inside the covenant as apostate Jerusalem. The book's own common-view note signals this as a deliberate replacement of the standard referent, not a refinement of its boundary.
rationale: Although the book preserves the thematic vocabulary of 'bondage,' it replaces the consensus's central referent. Every blind response identifies Egypt primarily as the world/sin external to God's people; the book identifies it primarily as covenant Jerusalem in corruption, building on Rev 11:8's 'great city... where also our Lord was crucified.' Response A does list an apostate-Jerusalem reading of Rev 11:8 as a minority alternative, so the book is not NOVEL—the position is recognizable within the interpretive landscape—but elevating it to the primary meaning contradicts the consensus core rather than narrowing it, because accepting 'Egypt = covenant city' requires rejecting 'Egypt = the world out of which God's people are redeemed' as the governing identification. Extension is a partial reclassification: bondage-cases remain, but they are transferred from the pagan world to the covenant community.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the book keeps the consensus category of 'bondage' and merely restricts the symbol's application to the Revelation 11:8 usage, where even a listed minority consensus alternative already identifies the city as apostate Jerusalem; on that reading the book narrows the extension without replacing the category. This is a serious objection, but it understates that the book's entry offers the covenant-city identification as the primary meaning of the term, displacing rather than qualifying the world/sin referent.
